entry.title: NFC South Week 5 Review: The picture remains muddy
entry.summary: The division saw more losses than wins this week. With the Panthers on their bye week, the Buccaneers pulled off a primetime upset, while the Falcons found themselves on the opposite end of that scenario. The Saints continue to stink. Here’s the Week 5 NFC South Review. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) Week 5 Result: Buccaneers […]
entry.content:
The division saw more losses than wins this week. With the Panthers on their bye week, the Buccaneers pulled off a primetime upset, while the Falcons found themselves on the opposite end of that scenario. The Saints continue to stink.

Here’s the Week 5 NFC South Review.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4)

Week 5 Result: Buccaneers 24 – Cowboys 16
Week 6 Opponent:  Pittsburgh Steelers

The Buccaneers desperately needed a win, and UDFA Jalon Daniels delivered in primetime. It wasn’t a pretty win; the Cowboys practically gave the game away with a smorgasbord of mental mistakes and turnovers, but a win is a win.

The Buccaneers hardly feel like a threat sitting at 1-4, and their odds of winning the division are still low, but they are no longer staring down the barrel of a winless season. They’ll host a Steelers team missing multiple starting WRs, giving them a good shot at another victory.

New Orleans Saints (1-4)

Week 5 Result: Saints 13 – Vikings 23 
Week 6 Opponent: New York Giants

After the Falcons throttled them in Week 4, the Vikings buried the Saints in Week 5. Tyler Shough failed to throw for 100 yards and threw two interceptions, bringing his turnover total to 10. Shough is currently the most pressured QB through all games played. The Saints defense breathed life into a middling Vikings offense, which scored two touchdowns after going weeks without one.

This was supposed to be the season Kellen Moore’s team put it all together, but they were more discombobulated than ever. They’ll travel to the Big Apple to take on a Giants team that is coming off a tie after a vintage Dan Quinn moment.

Carolina Panthers (2-2)

Week 5 Result: Bye Week
Week 6 Opponent: Philadelphia Eagles

The Panthers couldn’t have asked for a better result during their bye week. Their two biggest threats in the division (Atlanta and New Orleans) both failed to win, and Carolina now sits alone in first place. Sometimes an early bye works against a team, but this one came at a good time for the hobbled Panthers.

They’re hoping to get a few players back heading into Week 6. The Panthers will travel to Philadelphia to take on an Eagles team suffering from a 3-game losing streak.

Atlanta Falcons (2-3)

Week 5 Result: Falcons 23 – Ravens 30
Week 6 Opponent: Chicago Bears

The Falcons blew it in primetime. The team couldn’t stop the Ravens resurgence and faded from the fourth quarter into overtime. Multiple individual plays stand out, but there is plenty of blame to go around. Tommy Rees and Jeff Ulbrich both failed to adjust as the game went on. Michael Penix Jr. needs to hit his layup passes at a higher rate; doing so would’ve helped seal the game.

It sounds like Penix rib injury isn’t too serious, which is good news because the Falcons will host the Bears. It also sounds like this will be Caleb Williams’ return game, but the Bears secondary can be picked apart.

Three teams are sitting below .500, and the division leader is sitting right at it. It’s a marathon, not a sprint, but the division is limping out of the gate.

entry.title: Reports: Michael Penix Jr. rib injury does not seem to be serious, status for Week 6 still up in the air
entry.summary: Michael Penix Jr. couldn’t finish the Sunday Night Football loss to the Baltimore Ravens after getting drilled in the ribs late; he actually returned briefly after Tua Tagoviloa took the field for a single play but was in too much pain to return for overtime. The worry was that Penix, who despite some very real […]
entry.content:
Michael Penix Jr. couldn’t finish the Sunday Night Football loss to the Baltimore Ravens after getting drilled in the ribs late; he actually returned briefly after Tua Tagoviloa took the field for a single play but was in too much pain to return for overtime. The worry was that Penix, who despite some very real hiccups against Baltimore has given this passing game a massive boost over the past three weeks, might miss a game or multiple games owing to his injury.

The team hasn’t confirmed this yet, but Adam Schefter reports that it’s a relatively minor rib injury—as minor as those get, given that they’re not particularly fun to go through—and Penix may actually be able to start in Week 6. The days ahead will tell the tale.

This is a relief for multiple reasons. The first is that you could tell when he took the hit that Penix was hurt, and the fact that Tagovailoa had to finish the game meant we were bracing for Atlanta’s starter to be out a while. Ideally he would not miss the Chicago game given that the Bears have a very gettable pass defense, but even if he does, the fact that this doesn’t seem likely to stretch out multiple weeks is a major relief. The second is that not having Penix on the field opens the door to a horror show of backup quarterback options headlined by Tua, who has as many interceptions in three passes (1) as Penix has in three weeks and 77 attempts. Perhaps Tagovailoa will look a lot better not having to come into the game cold, but I’m not particularly eager to find out.

Kevin Stefanski said he’ll likely have an update on Wednesday, but it sounds like the Falcons and Penix may have dodged a more serious, long-term outcome here. We’ll learn more as the week rolls on.

Several things did not go according to plan in this one. Matthews played after there was some question of that this week, but he and Lindstrom had their worst games of the season against a tough Baltimore front. That led to a faltering ground game and more pressure than Penix was comfortable with. Every offensive lineman allowed at least one pressure, but those were heavily concentrated with Matthews (3) and Lindstrom (4), who allowed seven of the 12 pressures Penix faced on the day. When the line is struggling, the offense is going to splutter, as it did for long stretches Sunday night.

Otherwise, the usage shouldn’t look unfamiliar here. The Falcons run a lot of two tight end looks, Dotson is heavily favored as the team’s #2 receiver, and Zaccheaus is running ahead of Branch as WR3. The lack of production from Zaccheaus and Branch’s explosiveness in his limited looks may change that in the weeks ahead, however.

Several things went awry here, too. The first was simple wear and tear, as the Falcons had to lean very heavily on Samson Ebukam and Cameron Thomas in this one and taxed their defensive front, leading to a late collapse. The second is that an injury to CJ Henderson, who has playing quite well, put an enormous strain on this cornerback group, where Mike Hughes was already struggling to the tune of 5/8 for 63 yards (a significant portion of the 24/30 for 201 yards Tyler Huntley put up). When Hughes briefly exited the game, the Falcons had to put Mike Ford on the field, and the Ravens immediately went after him for a seven yard touchdown.

Hughes’ struggles have been well-documented at this point—he’s allowed a team-high 288 yards and two touchdowns with zero pass breakups and zero interceptions on 20 receptions and 29 targets—but Henderson had been a bright spot filling in for Terrell. If he’s out, the Falcons are heavily relying on rookie Aveion Terrell, Billy Bowman Jr., and some combination of Ford and practice squad elevations along with Hughes, which is a recipe for a tough week against the Bears.

The other note of note is that Daniels was once again in the driver’s seat for major snaps next to Divine Deablo, and it’s purely a situational timeshare with Harold Perkins Jr. The more a team runs, the more playing time Daniels receives, while Perkins gets more run against teams that pass heavily. It’s mostly working quite well.

The bad news: The Falcons were penalized three separate times on Sunday, each one costing them field position in a game where drives frequently sputtered out. The lack of discipline is showing up week after week on teams, and it’s proving costly week after week.

entry.title: Falcons vs. Ravens recap: Ghosts converge on Atlanta in an overtime loss
entry.summary: We knew that even a banged-up Ravens team would be a tough out for the surging Falcons, but that Atlanta could increase their chances of a win by playing a clean game that played to their considerable strengths. That’s not what we got. Instead, the offense looked shaky throughout the first quarter and into the […]
entry.content:
We knew that even a banged-up Ravens team would be a tough out for the surging Falcons, but that Atlanta could increase their chances of a win by playing a clean game that played to their considerable strengths. That’s not what we got.

Instead, the offense looked shaky throughout the first quarter and into the second quarter, with iffy run blocking and Michael Penix Jr. running ice cold. The Falcons defense forced a fumble that Jessie Bates took to the house to give Atlanta the lead, and Penix did get untracked in the second quarter to lead a productive drive. But the Falcons fought field position issues caused by multiple special teams penalties, struggled to consistently pick up yardage on the ground, had notable miscues in run defense, and tried to get a little too cute on key fourth down and red zone plays in ways that ended up harming the effort. The Ravens, who kept settling for field goals and sticking with what they knew they could do with Tyler Huntley under center and talented backs to bring to bear, made this a tense game as a result even as Jeff Ulbrich kept them at bay and held to 15 points through three quarters. It seemed like the Falcons would still cruise to a win when they went up eight points with not much time left in the fourth quarter, but instead Huntley found endless success on passes over the middle against a gassed defense, including a touchdown, and then Derrick Henry converted the two point try to tie things up. The Falcons, with 40 seconds left, couldn’t get close enough for a field goal try in regulation.

That left overtime, and a gassed defense down CJ Henderson kept showing cracks as Huntley and Henry marched down the field. Jeff Ulbrich has had answers for just about everything this year, but as the game wore on, unproductive blitzes and iffy run defense came to doom Atlanta. That left Tua Tagovailoa, in for an injured Penix, to try to lead a heroic drive down the field to tie things up or win outright down 30-23. He connected on a nice ball over the middle to Drake London and then immediately threw an interception to end things. It felt like a game the Falcons would lose as soon as the Ravens got deep into Atlanta territory late in the fourth quarter, and one of the nastiest things I can say about this game is that it felt extremely familiar.

Ghosts converged on this team from every angle. The shoddy run defense that cost them repeatedly in 2025 was especially costly against a Baltimore team that knows how to run the ball. Penix’s familiar problems with pressure and accuracy, which were largely absent the past two weeks, cost the team opportunities in a way that also proved costly. Mike Hughes’ coverage struggles and the team’s depth woes at cornerback, the former which has been consistent and the latter which we hoped was a thing of the past, hit hard, though in fairness this defense was never going to be in great shape down both A.J. Terrell and CJ Henderson. Coordinators trying things that either outright don’t work or offer quickly diminishing returns played a role in this loss, too, and you can see apparitions of Zac Robinson, Jimmy Lake, Dean Pees, Dirk Koetter, and so forth floating in the air as I type that. This team lost in large part because they were spiritually if not exactly like the Falcons team that have struggled so much in the recent past.

What you make of this loss likely depends on what you made of the Falcons coming into this game, and what you thought Baltimore was capable of with Huntley at quarterback. If you thought Atlanta was showing signs of being a playoff-caliber team after their two beatdowns of Green Bay and New Orleans, this will be a bitter effort to reckon with, especially if you believed the Ravens were not going to be up to snuff with so many backups in. If you thought the Falcons hadn’t faced a true test yet and the Ravens were still one of the league’s better teams even with a backup quarterback and fourth-string center in, this one will sting, but likely only a little.

Either way, the Falcons have fallen back under .500, Penix is hurt (though we don’t know how badly yet), there are fresh questions and familiar questions about everything from the run defense to Jake Matthews to the secondary, and this team is back on the roller coaster we fervently hoped they had hopped off after the past two weeks. They’re neither as bad as they looked the first two weeks nor as good as they looked the last two, but if this ends up representing what this team looks like in the middle of those two poles, it’s going to be another bumpy sort of season.

On to the full recap.

The Good

  • Michael Penix Jr. is streaky. He started this game ice cold, not just missing passes but missing them badly, and the offense suffered as a result. He followed that up with a second quarter drive where he caught fire, heaving bombs to Drake London and Jahan Dotson and zipping a pass by two Ravens for a Kyle Pitts touchdown. When he’s on, he can make heroic throws downfield at a rate not many quarterbacks in this league can match, and he was on enough to give this team a fighting chance until quite late.
  • Bijan Robinson had a run in the first quarter that left me speechless, where he seemed dead in the backfield and turned around and ripped off a 15 yard run thanks to agility, toughness, and good old-fashioned magic. On a day where Brian Robinson Jr. couldn’t get any breathing room, Bijan put up a tidy five-plus yards per carry and got 86 yards on 17 carries. He probably should have had more touches, honestly, even though there were plenty of unproductive runs along the way. I give him an enormous amount of credit for the sheer effort on a bad Penix throw on the final Falcons drive of regulation, too, even though he couldn’t quite get it.
  • I think Penix would throw the ball to Drake London if he was deep in the Pacific Ocean and Penix was on the 35 yard line in Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The level of trust between those two is unreal, and London made huge third down grabs for first downs over and over again in this one, seemingly willing himself open just enough for Penix to laser passes in there to him. London is a great receiver who just needs competent quarterback play to produce like one, and with Penix he has a quarterback who is never going to be afraid to target him.
  • Jahan Dotson can fly, and Michael Penix Jr. loves slinging that ball downfield. That’s looking like it’ll be a fruitful combination this year, as Penix hit him for a beautiful deep touchdown in Week 4 and got him on a 36 yard bomb that set up a Falcons score in the second quarter.
  • Kyle Pitts was going to get involved, and after he lumbered to life a bit in Week 4, he arrived in Week 5. A nice grab and run in the second quarter was a prelude to a touchdown grab to finish off that drive.
  • Samson Ebukam has been a really good signing, and he flashed again in this one. His play of the game was the big third down, third quarter sack of Tyler Huntley, putting a swift end to a Baltimore drive when they were down just two points.
  • Ditto Jared Ivey, who has been in and out of the rotation at outside linebacker but had an early sack in this one where he fought through a defender around his .
  • Cameron Thomas got a half sack and Gervon Dexter got none, but they were the team’s two most consistently impactful defenders up front from my point of view. Dexter was relentless in pursuit and caught a couple of run plays from behind, while Thomas was one of the few Falcons who consistently made Huntley uncomfortable on Sunday night.
  • Kendal Daniels was not always stellar against the run—I saw a couple of iffy angles—but his tackling was mostly incredibly sound, he was getting his hand up constantly and managed to tip a pass, and he looked confident and rangy out there against Baltimore. When teams want to run the ball more, Daniels is the go-to guy next to Divine Deablo, and there’s a good reason for that.
  • Sydney Brown delivered a good hit to jar the ball loose from Mark Andrews, which gave Atlanta’s defense a chance to make a big play. Jessie Bates took advantage and authored his latest in a long line of big plays, scooping up the fumble and taking it to the house to open up the scoring for Atlanta.
  • Nick Folk started off the season in rough fashion, and I still don’t know the exact range at which the Falcons stop trusting his leg. But in this one, they gave him short tries and a 48 yarder and he banged them home comfortably each time. If the game had come down to his leg in the end, I think the Falcons would’ve gladly given him the shot, but they couldn’t get close enough for him to work.

The Ugly

  • Penix is streaky. He started this one missing layups, is now an abysmal 1-0f-16 passing when pressured, and is not a credible threat to scramble for more than a handful of yards. At his worst in this one, he was inaccurate and hesitant, and then he took a big hit near the end of regulation that ultimately knocked him out for overtime. The familiar pressure struggles, accuracy woes on gimme throws, and injury concerns are all there even if Penix (hopefully) does not miss time next week, and while Chicago’s anemic defense gives him a chance for a get-right game, it’s really important for Penix and this offense to find easy buttons against pressure and achieve more consistency so brilliant stretches and games aren’t followed up by costly moments and lackluster efforts. Inconsistency is, at least at the moment, a defining feature for both quarterback and team.
  • Tua Tagovailoa finally got into a game when Penix got hurt and completed two of three passes, getting rid of the ball quickly and decisively. Twice that worked out well, as he completed a pair of passes for 34 yards, including a zippy ball downfield to Drake London to kick off Atlanta’s overtime drive. The problem was that he very confidently and quickly threw a gimme interception on that third pass that ended Atlanta’s faint gleam of hope in overtime. If Tua has to start, he can’t be throwing those.
  • The offensive line didn’t do a great job. Atlanta barely cleared 100 yards rushing and most of that was due to herculean efforts by Bijan, as he and Brian Robinson Jr. were repeatedly hit shortly after getting the handoff and well before the line of scrimmage. In addition, Penix ate three sacks—some of them owing to his own delay, to be fair—and saw a lot more pressure tonight as Atlanta’s chips failed frequently and Jake Matthews in particular just kept getting smoked. Matthews, you’ll note, has $20 million in dead money next year after the Falcons have continually tacked on extra years to his deal to free up space elsewhere, but he’s going to have to find his footing (and potentially better health, given that he was playing after getting hurt last week) quickly to avoid becoming a real anchor on this offense. That’s not to excuse the overall effort from this line, which was lackluster against a fearsome Ravens front.
  • The Falcons brought plenty of pressure but just couldn’t convert it to many sacks, a credit to how quick Tyler Huntley is to get away from pressure and get rid of the ball. That has been somewhat of a theme early on this year, where this pass rush is impacting the game but not consistently closing those plays out. That should come with time, but it gave the Ravens a fighting chance at keeping drives going that they unfortunately capitalized on, with Huntley making a couple of back-breaking throws after evading multiple defenders. He’s an underrated backup, but the Falcons made better quarterbacks in Jordan Love and Tyler Shough very uncomfortable, and the fact that they let Huntley go for a tidy 201 yards and two touchdowns while going 21/32 is bad. There’s no putting a coating of sugar on that one.
  • This Falcons run defense had been very good thus far, but they did have a couple of cupcake matchups on the schedule along the way. The Ravens figured to be their toughest challenge and were right out of the gate, with Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, and even Zay Flowers gashing them for major gains on the opening drive. The Falcons did start to settle in, but Henry is a tough matchup and he looked like it throughout the first half. Things felt apart spectacularly on the Ravens’ opening drive of the third quarter, with Justice Hill breaking loose for over 50 yards to set up a score and Henry running wild in the second half against an increasingly gassed defense. We knew the Falcons probably were not the best run defense in the league, but they looked awful on balance Sunday night, allowing over 200 yards to the Ravens and wilting especially badly late. Chicago has to be licking their chops next week with their talented set of backs.
  • Special teams has yet to fully gel as a strength, to put it mildly. In this one, the Falcons committed three separate costly penalties—two holds and an unnecessary roughness—that left them with dismal field position to start their drives. Given the margin in this one, the extra yards Atlanta had to travel were certainly a factor in the outcome.
  • I didn’t think this coaching staff did a stellar job in this game, something I think they’d echo. Kevin Stefanski’s job is to get this team ready and they looked sluggish and off-balance far too often yesterday evening. Tommy Rees’ job is to make life as easy as possible for this offense and I think he fell short of that with the deletion of the run game inside the red zone, plays like the Jake Matthews touchdown attempt (a fun surprise but not the guy you want to entrust with having to catch the ball in the end zone), and a lack of quick looks for Penix. I definitely thought Jeff Ulbrich, who was working with real limitations after CJ Henderson exited the game, could not come up with answers against the run and resorted to blitzing late when it simply wasn’t working against Huntley, who simply and quickly found the man left open over and over again. With penalties and errors of execution certainly playing a major role, I’m not going to kill the staff for this one, but I think it’s fair to argue they were part of the problem.
  • I’ll single out that Matthews touchdown attempt as a defining play for this game, in fact. Matthews was not a sure thing to play in this game and is notably not a receiver in any capacity, with zero career receptions on a single target coming into tonight. The Falcons got the look they wanted as Matthews got open, which is a credit to Rees for drawing it up, but you have to peel back one additional layer and ask whether against a team like the Ravens you really want Matthews having to make a grab to be your scoring play. Penix put the ball a tick too high but was going over a defender there, which meant it was all on Matthews being able to go up and reel that in rather than the Falcons simply trying to go to London or, I dunno, one of their collection of several tight ends who do have experience catching the ball. That’s a play that’s fun to try out against a lesser squad but has too many possible failure points to be a red zone look against Baltimore.
  • One of the most important things—perhaps the most important thing—besides wins and losses this year is whether the Falcons can show us they are a different football team than the mediocre, collapse-prone squad that muddled through a series of 7-10 and 8-9 seasons in recent years. The Carolina blowout can be waved away a little if you’re so inclined because of just how awful Cooper Rush was in that game, but that effort and last night’s were vintage Falcons games for different reasons. This one saw the Falcons surrender leads, wilt defensively late, and make too many mistakes across the board to earn the win, and I could have and did write that series of statements dozens of times in different permutations over the past eight seasons. When we look back at the end of the 2026 season, if this loss is emblematic of what the Falcons proved to be over 17 games, this regime will have gotten off to a rocky start.

The Wrapup

Game MVP

Drake London, who simply vacuumed up every target sent his way and kept the Falcons alive over and over again. This game would not have been this close if not for his superlative effort, so he earns the honors.

One Takeaway

The Falcons are going to be an up-and-down team this year because they have unpredictability baked into their quarterback position and enough trouble spots (Matthews, Mike Hughes, potentially the run defense, special teams) that it seems as though it will be difficult for them to sustain stellar play. Let’s hope this one ages poorly.

Next Week

For the first time in nearly a month, the Falcons aren’t in primetime. They’ll be up against the Chicago Bears, possibly getting back Caleb Williams after a couple of rough weeks.

Final Word

DisappointingandIstayeduptoolateforit.

entry.title: Week 5 Snap Reactions: A late collapse dooms Falcons
entry.summary: Dear Reader, I regret to inform you that the Atlanta Falcons blew a fourth-quarter lead and lost in overtime to the Baltimore Ravens. Here are the Week 5 Snap Reactions. The Defensive Dam Broke The Falcons defense came undone. After playing sound defense for roughly 3 quarters, Jeff Ulbrich’s unit couldn’t keep up with the […]
entry.content:
Dear Reader, I regret to inform you that the Atlanta Falcons blew a fourth-quarter lead and lost in overtime to the Baltimore Ravens. Here are the Week 5 Snap Reactions.

The Defensive Dam Broke

The Falcons defense came undone. After playing sound defense for roughly 3 quarters, Jeff Ulbrich’s unit couldn’t keep up with the Ravens adjustments in the 4th. After not blitzing much this season, Ulbrich turned up the heat, and it worked at first.

However, the blitz stopped working toward the end of the game. The Falcons generated only one pressure on 12 dropbacks during the Ravens final two drives, per NFLPro. The unit looked exhausted on the overtime drive, and injuries finally caught up with them.

Early Down Struggles

Late-down heroics are unsustainable; the Falcons faced too many 3rd and long situations on offense. While the 9-5 connection bailed them out most of the game, it couldn’t when the Falcons needed to sustain drives late in the game.

Credit to Jesse Minter; his defense had answers for Tommy Rees on early downs, and the young OC couldn’t adjust. Bijan hit over 100 scrimmage yards yet again, but Minter forcing Atlanta to win with Penix’s arm on 3rd down eventually paid off.

The Devil is in the Details

A Jake Matthews drop, a wide-open Bijan missed, and Zay Flowers running through Divine Deablo. It’s the little things that come back to bite you. Penix is still struggling to hit the easy passes, and unlike the previous two weeks, the run game couldn’t overcome those misses. With the season Matthews is having as a blocker and him dealing with an injury all week, I can’t imagine why they used that play now; yes, he should’ve caught the ball, but Matthews not timing a jump correctly isn’t surprising, considering he’s not a skill player. Rees got too cute, and with the options he has on offense, we haven’t seen enough opportunities for the players paid to catch the ball.

What is Michael Penix Jr.?

Is he a franchise QB? Is he done after this year? Are the injuries too much to bear? The reality is, there are still a lot of games left this season before we can reach a final verdict. As it stands, his footwork is still a problem, causing him to miss too many easy opportunities; that and his inability to access multiple arm angles—he’s stiff as a board.

He can make the difficult throws scouts drool over, but routinely botches the layups. These things matter more to me than the rib injury because a better throw to Bijan late in the game prevents that injury from ever happening, and these issues exist regardless of injury. His future is uncertain, and if he can’t work through these problems, the team won’t view him as the answer under center.

Atlanta now sits at 2-3, back under .500 yet again. Penix’s ribs will be monitored, but the team is reeling from injuries across the board, an excuse that’s hard to swallow after losing to the Ravens sans Lamar Jackson. Kevin Stefanski and his will have their work cut out for them as they hit a tough two-game stretch against some of the NFC’s best.

entry.title: Falcons – Ravens instant recap: The overtime letdown in primetime
entry.summary: The depleted Ravens are still a dangerous team, something we received an all-too-potent reminder of on Sunday Night Football. The Falcons had plenty of advantages—they were at home, red hot, and had their starting quarterback, to name a few—but couldn’t summon the kind of clean, hyper-effective game they needed to win comfortably. In the end, […]
entry.content:
The depleted Ravens are still a dangerous team, something we received an all-too-potent reminder of on Sunday Night Football. The Falcons had plenty of advantages—they were at home, red hot, and had their starting quarterback, to name a few—but couldn’t summon the kind of clean, hyper-effective game they needed to win comfortably. In the end, they couldn’t even summon up the kind of effort they needed to win, period.

Atlanta struggled with penalties, with three on special teams leaving them with poor field position and penalties on offense and defense complicating drives. They struggled with sometimes iffy play calling, like overly cute screens and a would-be touchdown pass to Jake Matthews, or blitzes late in the game that left targets open for Tyler Huntley, who was getting passes out at lightning speed. Combined with missed tackles, poor angles, and the Ravens executing their gameplan extremely well all game, the Falcons simply didn’t have enough in the tank to win this one, with the game coming down to Tua Tagovailoa’s arm after Michael Penix Jr. was injured late and ending on a Tua interception. After two straight beatdowns of the Packers and Saints, it was a bracing effort that tells us that well-coached, quality football teams can exploit Atlanta’s extant weaknesses and uncover new ones. There’s a lot to work on this week, and there isn’t a soul in Flowery Branch who is unaware of that. Now it’s time to see how the Falcons respond and recover from this latest gut punch.

Here’s a drive-by-drive recap of the game you just watched.

1st Quarter

The Falcons chose to defer, and the Ravens went out from the 30. An end-around to Zay Flowers picked up 12 yards after he got nice blocking and the Falcons bit on the other side. Derrick Henry then picked up seven yards up the middle. A quick throw to Justice Hill was bobbled and ultimately dropped. Hill then took a carry up the middle and picked up another big first down. Henry then stumbled through a tackle attempt and picked up another seven yards. Tyler Huntley then got away from pressure and got his receiver for a first down and 11 yards. Mike Hughes then got low on Henry to stop him just shy of a touchdown. Henry then took it out of the wildcat but was decisively stopped by the Falcons run defense for a loss, and an illegal formation penalty would’ve backed the Ravens up had it been accepted. Huntley then tried to hit Mark Andrews and it went through his hands after a bad snap. Tyler Loop was good on the short field goal, though, to make it 3-0 Ravens.

Olamide Zaccheaus had a solid return backed up by a holding call on Jammie Robinson, so the Falcons started from about their own 15 yard line. Michael Penix Jr. then tried to fire on downfield to Drake London but it was well behind and knocked down by the defender. Bijan Robinson then picked up four yards up the middle. Penix then felt pressure and threw one backpedaling and hit a Ravens defender in the helmet. Punt.

Henry then ran easily for a first down. On the next play, Jared Ivey did a great job fighting through a blocker wrapped around his ankle to sack Tyler Huntley. Then Sydney Brown forced Mark Andrews to fumble on a catch, Jessie Bates scooped it up, and Bates returned it all the way for a touchdown. 7-3 Falcons.

Henry took his first handoff for nearly 10 yards. A direct snap to almost Henry got a first down before LaCale London tackled him. Huntley then snuck it for a yard. Huntley tried to throw it to Henry under duress, but Kendal Daniels got his hand up and knocked it away. A toss to Justice Hill looked like it was on its way to a first down, but he slipped for five yards. On third and five, Brandon Dorlus and company arrived and dropped Henry for a small loss. Punt.

Bijan Robinson had a jaw-dropping run where he looked dead in the backfield and somehow not only escaped but picked up about 15 yards and a first down. Unreal stuff. A three yard carry for Robinson followed, and then Penix under pressure threw it in the dirt near London. Penix then got away from pressure and scrambled for about five yards after slight hesitation, but didn’t quite get the first. Punt, and a good one from Jake Bailey.

Huntley hit Flowers over the middle for six yards. Henry rolled forward for two yards. A quick pass to Devontez Walker just picked up a first down. Henry then took it nine yards.

2nd Quarter

Henry then got a first down. A neutral zone infraction from Za’Darius Smith gave the Ravens five more yards. Huntley tried to scramble away from Daniels, but was stopped after a minimal gain. Divine Deablo then got Henry after a couple of yards. Huntley tried to get Flowers, but he dropped it and the ball fell incomplete. After a delay of game in service of trying and failing to get the Falcons to jump offsides, they punted it and Zaccheaus returned it for about eight yards. Another holding call brought them back near their own end zone.

Brian Robinson Jr. took it for a couple of yards, following that up right another couple of yards. With pressure showing up immediately, Penix slung it into the ground near London. Bailey punted out of his own end zone to about the Ravens 40, and Baltimore picked up six yards on the return.

A quick pass from Huntley to a tight end picked up close to 15 yards after a long rumble. Henry then got hit early but still picked up close to four yards. A snap to Flowers, who was looking to throw, was brought down by Zach Harrison with an assist from Cameron Thomas. A short screen pass fell well short of a first down after Gervon Dexter caught up with the receiver from behind. Loop hit from 51 yards to make it 7-6 Falcons.

Zaccheaus got crushed at the 20 on the kick return to set up poor field position again. Penix was waiting for something to open up downfield and took the sack. A screen to Kyle Pitts went for about 15 yards. Penix then uncorked one down the sideline to London, who got 17 yards. Bijan then went inside left and picked up five yards. Brian Robinson Jr. then went nowhere on second down as the defense swarmed him. Jahan Dotson then flew downfield and reeled in a deep ball from Penix that got the Falcons inside the red zone. Bijan then lost a couple of yards on first down. Penix then hit Bijan on a short route over the middle that went for a few yards. Then Penix fired one in to Pitts for a touchdown. 14-6 Falcons.

A return to the 37 yard line was brought back by a hold. Huntley then connected on a low ball for a first down. Huntley then connected on a short pass that went for about five yards. A quick pass (again) to Flowers was about a yard shy of the first down. Huntley then snuck it and somehow stayed on his feet for 12 yards. On the next play, Huntley had to get rid of it under pressure, and a holding call backed up Baltimore. On the next play, Huntley got rid of it milliseconds before Cameron Thomas destroyed him. He then connected for nine yards, and got away from pressure to get Bateman for a first down. Huntley got away from a sack and then threw it away. Huntley then was a little too high on a downfield shot and it fell incomplete, with Hughes close by. A false start backed the Ravens up five yards. The Ravens then burned a handful of seconds on a kneel and left one second for Tyler Loop’s third attempt of the game, and he hit from 51 yards again. 14-9 Falcons at the end of the first half.

3rd Quarter

After a touchback took the Falcons to the 35 yard line, Bijan’s opening carry picked up five yards. A Jake Matthews false start then erased that gain. Penix dodged multiple defenders on the next play for a gain of perhaps a yard. Then Penix connected with Pitts for 12 yards and a first down. Bijan then got around a tackle attempt for nine yards. He then plunged ahead for a couple of yards and a first down. Bijan then took a carry 37 yards on a truly crazy run to get the Falcons close. He lost a yard or so on the next carry as the Ravens defense swarmed. The Falcons then tried to do something silly, with Penix throwing to Jake Matthews, but Matthews couldn’t come up with it. Then Penix overthrew Dotson a bit in the end zone, which brought Nick Folk on for the short field goal try. 17-9 Falcons.

The Ravens returned it to the 26 yard line. Derrick Henry took one to the sideline for three yards. Huntley then fired one to Flowers, who was tackled by Cameron Thomas just shy of a first down. Justice Hill then slipped through the line and ran it for about 50 yards, getting the Ravens within striking distance. Henry was then tackled for no gain. A screen pass to Henry got good blocking and Henry did the rest for a touchdown. The Ravens then tried for a two point conversion, but Andrews couldn’t hold on to it. 17-15 Falcons.

Brian Robinson Jr. took the kick return past the 35 yard line. Bijan then ran for no gain, with Kyle Hamilton down on the play. Penix then hit Bijan for a 10 yard pickup and a first down. A quick sideline ball to Bijan picked up three yards, and then Brian Robinson Jr. picked up four more yards on the ground. BRJ then took it for maybe a yard, setting up a 4th and 2. Penix had almost immediate pressure and threw it low for Charlie Woerner, who grabbed it short of a first down. Turnover on downs.

Henry picked up three yards on first down. Huntley got away from pressure again and picked up three yards on a scramble after evading multiple defenders. On third down, Samson Ebukam had a relentless rush, got ahold of Huntley, and took him down for a sack. Punt, and Branch returned it about ten yards. An unnecessary roughness call on the Falcons brought them back considerably.

Bijan picked up four yards on first down. Brian Robinson got another four yards on the next carry. Penix then found London for a short pass, and London vaulted over a defender to about 10 yards.

4th Quarter

Pitts took the short swing pass for about five yards. An offensive lineman got pushed right into Bijan’s lap on the next carry for a loss. Penix then found London again on the sideline for another first down. On a would-be screen to Branch, he already had a defender on him and lost 13 yards. Penix then scrambled for a handful of yards. Penix then found London again for a first down. Bijan took it three yards, and then Penix got Pitts for six more yards. Then Penix got London againnnnn for another first down. Bijan got a yard on the next play. Penix then tried to get Pitts over the middle but didn’t get him after contact between Pitts and a defender that was initially flagged and then picked up. Penix was then hit as he threw trying to go to Dotson in the end zone. Nick Folk hit the 34 yard field goal try to make it 20-15 Falcons.

After a return past the 30, the Ravens gave Henry the opening handoff for four yards or so. Henry got ahead for a couple of yards before Jared Ivey got him. On third down, Huntley looked for Andrews and Xavier Watts knocked it loose with perfect timing. Punt, and a fair catch just inside the 20.

Penix hung on a bit until the pressure got too close and threw an off balance ball that was out too far for Brian Robinson Jr. to grab. Penix then threw it to Bijan but missed low. Penix then found Branch on what seemed to be an ill-advised throw well short of the sticks, but Branch put his man on skates and ran for a first down and more. Bijan got tackled for a loss of a yard by Calais Campbell. Penix hit London again for another first down, and then got Charlie Woerner on what seemed to be another dangerous ball that Woerner reeled in diving. A delayed handoff to Bijan picked up three yards, and Brian followed that up with a yard. Penix under pressure tried to throw it to Bijan but it was behind him and Bijan couldn’t scoop it out of the dirt. Nick Folk hit it from 48 yards out to make it 23-15 Falcons.

The Falcons got the stop on the return. Huntley had a solid scramble, but it came back owing to a hold. Huntley had forever in the pocket owing to a series of misses by Falcons pass rushers, and then pass interference on Watts added five yards after Zay Flowers caught the ball. Huntley then threw one to a diving Bateman for a first down. A quick pass over the middle went for about five yards. Huntley then got Bateman again for a first down. A quick pass to Andrews got three yards before Harold Perkins Jr. drove him backwards and got the tackle. Huntley then got Bateman again for a first down and more to put the Ravens in a first and goal situation, with Mike Hughes hurt on the play. Huntley then threw a touchdown pass to Devontez Walker. The Ravens quite sensibly decided to go for two points, and Henry got to the edge and scored, with Mike Hughes trying to get the tackle one-on-one and slipping. 23-23 tie with 40 seconds left.

The Falcons started from around their own 20. Penix found Dotson downfield for 20ish yards on a nice ball. On the next play, Penix hung on looking for a man downfield and a defender got away from Pitts and Bijan, with the ball squirting out before Ryan Neuzil fell on it. Penix was hurt on the play and Tua Tagovailoa entered the game. Tua then connected with Bijan for a solid gain to set up third and 6. Penix re-entered the game, and with a defender on his ankle simply threw the ball away. Punt, and the clock ran out.

Overtime

The Ravens elected to receive, and their kick return took them past the 30. Henry picked up nine yards to kick things off for Baltimore on the drive. On second down, Henry was stopped for a small loss by Dexter, who had been rolling. A quick shot to Andrews picked up about nine yards and a first down. Henry picked up four yards before he got stopped by Jessie Bates. On the next play, a quick pass to Justice Hill was stopped cold by Kendal Daniels after no gain. A quick pass to Flowers got a first down after Divine Deablo couldn’t bring him down short of the sticks. Huntley then scrambled for three yards before Daniels got him. Henry then powered through the pile to pick up 11 yards. A neutral zone infraction on LaCale London gave the Ravens another five yards. Then Henry got a yard. Then Huntley hit Bateman for a first down. Henry rolled for another seven yards. Andrews caught another first down at the four yard line. Henry took it to the one yard line, and then Huntley punched it in on the next play. 30-23 Ravens.

After a solid return, Tua was back in the game for an injured Penix and immediately connected with London on a big gainer over the middle of the field. Tua then threw an interception on the next pass to end the game.

entry.content:
It has been a tale of two game sample sizes thus far for Atlanta, and they’ve looked like the worst team in the league in two of those games and a playoff-caliber team in the other two. This Ravens game will be an excellent opportunity to prove that the wins over the Packers and Saints in Weeks 3 and 4 were indicative of who this team is and can be.

The Ravens are the best opponent Atlanta’s faced thus far, albeit diminished owing to injuries. They’re 3-1, a top 15 team in most measures you can think of and top ten in quite a few, and are loaded with talent. The injuries make the sledding a bit easier, but there’s little question this will require the Falcons to be sharp across the board.

Will they do it? I believe they can, at the very least. Please use this as your discussion thread and join your fellow fans as we find out. Go Falcons!

entry.title: Intriguing players to watch in Falcons vs. Ravens
entry.summary: The Atlanta Falcons cap a grueling three-game primetime stretch on Sunday Night Football when they host the Baltimore Ravens in their return to Mercedes-Benz Stadium. It marks Atlanta’s biggest test yet and their first 2026 battle against a winning team. As the Falcons look to prove their recent momentum is sustainable, five key contributors will […]
entry.content:
The Atlanta Falcons cap a grueling three-game primetime stretch on Sunday Night Football when they host the Baltimore Ravens in their return to Mercedes-Benz Stadium. It marks Atlanta’s biggest test yet and their first 2026 battle against a winning team. As the Falcons look to prove their recent momentum is sustainable, five key contributors will face their own tests come Sunday night.

Jake Matthews

Left tackle Jake Matthews’ test centers on his status for the game and whether he’ll be healthy enough to make his 200th consecutive NFL start against the Ravens while battling a groin injury. Last week’s win marked 200 career starts, but this week would be 200 in a row, as he hasn’t missed a game since Week 2 of 2014. It’s an incredible feat of endurance, durability, and consistency, and it would be a shame if it ended this weekend.

Zachariah Branch

For rookie wideout Zachariah Branch, the test is whether a heavier workload leads to a breakout. The Falcons have steadily gotten Branch more involved each week, dialing up manufactured screen touches and giving him more chances to stretch defenses with his speed. It seems only a matter of time before Branch evolves from a gadget weapon into a game-changing staple in the Falcons offense.

Cameron Thomas

With an edge-rusher room that is plagued by injuries, Cameron Thomas faces the toughest test of his breakout season. Thomas has been a pleasant surprise through the first month, but pressure will increase for him to carry the pass rush against the Ravens as others battle injuries. Thomas has feasted in recent weeks against mostly subpar competition, but Sunday night will bring a significant uptick against Ravens left tackle Ronnie Stanley. Testing himself against one of the league’s top pass protectors will help reveal if Thomas’ early-season tear is for real.

Billy Bowman and Sydney Brown

Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers will test both defensive backs, Billy Bowman and Sydney Brown. According to PFF, Flowers currently leads the NFL with 282 receiving yards when operating out of the slot. Bowman primarily mans the slot when the Falcons play nickel, while Brown handles those responsibilities when the team utilizes big nickel with a third safety instead of a cornerback. So far this year, the Falcons have relied more on big nickel when the opponent threatens to run the ball.

No rushing threat looms larger (literally) than Ravens running back Derrick Henry, so expect to see Brown matched up in the slot on early downs against Flowers. However, on obvious passing downs, Bowman will take over responsibilities for covering Flowers. Both players will need to pass the test of covering one of the NFL’s top receivers to keep a lid on Baltimore’s explosive potential.

Even without Lamar Jackson, Baltimore has enough firepower and challenges to reveal whether Atlanta’s recent turnaround is a temporary flash or a true foundation for 2026. Can you name other Falcons who will ultimately decide whether the team passes this Sunday night test?

entry.title: Atlanta Falcons uniforms: A complete history
entry.summary: Throughout their history, the Atlanta Falcons have undergone several uniform changes, from their original black jerseys and iconic red helmets in 1966 to the more modern designs of recent years. Some looks have become beloved classics, while others have sparked plenty of debate among fans. Whether it’s the classic red helmets, the black throwback jerseys, […]
entry.content:
Throughout their history, the Atlanta Falcons have undergone several uniform changes, from their original black jerseys and iconic red helmets in 1966 to the more modern designs of recent years. Some looks have become beloved classics, while others have sparked plenty of debate among fans.

Whether it’s the classic red helmets, the black throwback jerseys, or the uniforms worn during some of the franchise’s most memorable seasons, each era has brought something unique to Atlanta’s identity.

With that in mind, let’s take a look back at the complete history of the Falcons’ uniforms, how they’ve evolved over the years, and some of the memorable players and moments associated with each look.

1966-1970

The 1966 season marked the Atlanta Falcons’ inaugural year in the National Football League, and the team debuted with one of the more unique uniform combinations in the league. The original look featured black jerseys with white numbers outlined in red, white pants, and the now-iconic red helmets featuring the original Falcons logo. The away uniforms featured white jerseys with black numbers, while both combinations included distinctive red and black striping. It’s a classic look that remains a favorite among Falcons fans to this day.

One particularly interesting detail was the addition of two thin gold stripes on the helmets. As the story goes, the Falcons’ original uniforms looked a little too similar to those worn by the University of Georgia, which didn’t exactly sit well with their rivals at Georgia Tech. To keep everyone happy, the Falcons incorporated gold into the helmet striping as a nod to Georgia Tech, while maintaining the red and black associated with Georgia. The gold stripes remained through the 1969 season before being removed in 1970.

The uniforms also underwent a few minor adjustments in 1968, including the removal of the Falcons logo from the jersey sleeves in favor of additional striping. Otherwise, the original design remained largely unchanged throughout the franchise’s first five seasons.

Some of the most recognizable players to wear these uniforms included legendary linebacker Tommy Nobis, the Falcons’ first-ever draft pick, and Hall of Fame defensive end Claude Humphrey.

Although Atlanta struggled to find success on the field during its early years, these uniforms established the franchise’s identity. Decades later, the Falcons would bring back this classic combination as a throwback in 2009, proving that sometimes the original look is still one of the best.

1971-1977

The 1971 season brought the first major change to the Falcons’ uniforms, as the team ditched its original black home jerseys in favor of red. The new look featured red jerseys with white numbers outlined in black, along with updated sleeve striping and red socks. The Falcons kept their iconic red helmets and white pants, creating a simple yet classic look that would help define the franchise throughout the 1970s.

Although the switch from black to red was significant, the overall design remained relatively unchanged during this era. In fact, red would remain the Falcons’ primary home jersey color all the way through the 1989 season, making it one of the longest-lasting traditions in franchise history.

Notable players who wore these uniforms included quarterback Steve Bartkowski, wide receiver Alfred Jenkins, and defensive end Claude Humphrey. While the Falcons didn’t experience much postseason success during this period, these uniforms helped establish the red-and-black identity that fans still associate with the franchise today.

1978-1989

In 1978, the Falcons introduced another significant change to their uniforms, replacing their traditional white pants with silver ones. Personally, I’ve always liked the addition of silver, which became a staple of the Falcons’ color scheme through the 2002 season. The jerseys also received some updates, including more detailed collar and sleeve striping, the return of the Falcons logo to the sleeves, and a switch from black to red numbers on the white road jerseys.

Another notable change came in 1984, when the Falcons switched from white facemasks to black, a look that would remain part of the team’s identity for decades to come.

This era is perhaps best remembered by longtime Falcons fans for the team’s success during the 1980 season. Led by quarterback Steve Bartkowski, Atlanta finished 12–4, capturing its first division title and setting a franchise record for wins at the time. Other notable Falcons who wore these uniforms included running back Gerald Riggs and wide receiver Alfred Jenkins.

Although the team experienced its share of ups and downs throughout the 1980s, the combination of red jerseys, silver pants, and red helmets remains one of the more classic looks in Falcons history.

1990-1996

As the Falcons entered the 1990s, they decided it was time for a bold new look. The team brought back black jerseys as its primary home uniforms, but this time with a major twist: black helmets. For the first time in franchise history, Atlanta ditched its iconic red helmets in favor of an all-black look, signaling a new era for the franchise.

Red was almost entirely removed from the uniforms, appearing only as subtle accents around the numbers and along the stripes on the silver pants. The away uniforms also received a makeover, featuring black numbers and black socks to complement the new helmets. It was a simple, intimidating design that quickly became one of the most recognizable looks in Falcons history.

Of course, this era is also closely associated with one of the most electrifying players to ever wear a Falcons uniform: Deion “Prime Time” Sanders. Between Sanders’ unforgettable highlights and the team’s embrace of a new identity, these uniforms became synonymous with the Falcons of the early 1990s.

Although the design would undergo some minor changes in the years that followed, the introduction of the black helmet helped establish a look that would remain a defining part of the franchise’s identity for decades to come.

1997-2002

In 1997, the Falcons made some subtle improvements to their uniforms, bringing back a little more red to a look that had become predominantly black and white. While the home uniforms remained largely unchanged, the away jerseys once again featured red numbers, along with the return of red socks. It wasn’t a revolutionary redesign by any means, but the added red helped bring back some of the franchise’s original identity.

This era also featured some of the greatest moments in Falcons history up to that point. Most notably, the legendary 1998 “Dirty Birds” team, led by head coach Dan Reeves and running back Jamal Anderson, shocked the NFL by finishing 14–2 and advancing to the franchise’s first-ever Super Bowl appearance. Although Atlanta ultimately fell to the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XXXIII, that season remains one of the most memorable in team history.

The Falcons also made history during the 2002 playoffs, becoming the first visiting team to defeat the Green Bay Packers in a postseason game at Lambeau Field. Led by a young Michael Vick, Atlanta pulled off a stunning 27–7 victory, ending Green Bay’s previously perfect home playoff record.

Between the unforgettable Dirty Birds and Vick’s emergence as one of the NFL’s most exciting young quarterbacks, it’s safe to say these uniforms hold a special place in the hearts of many Falcons fans.

2003-2008

Ahead of the 2003 season, the Falcons underwent one of the most revolutionary changes in franchise history, completely redesigning their uniforms and, for the first time since their inception in 1966, introducing a new primary logo. The updated logo featured a sleeker, more aggressive-looking falcon, incorporating red and silver accents while resembling the letter “F.” The uniforms themselves also received a modern makeover, featuring a new number font, bold striping, and several different combinations.

For the first time in franchise history, the Falcons also introduced an alternate jersey, giving the team three options: black, red, and white. Initially, black remained the primary home jersey, with red serving as the alternate. However, in 2004, the Falcons reversed course, making red their primary home color and moving black to the alternate rotation.

The Falcons experimented with several combinations, including all-black uniforms and white jerseys paired with black pants. Personally, I think these were some of the cleanest combinations the franchise has ever worn. Unfortunately, the black pants disappeared following the 2008 season, bringing an end to one of the more underrated looks in Falcons history.

Of course, this era is also remembered for Michael Vick, whose electrifying playing style made him one of the most recognizable players in the NFL. For many fans, these uniforms will always be associated with Vick’s incredible highlights and the excitement surrounding the Falcons during the mid-2000s.

2009-2019

During the 2009 season, the Falcons went back to basics. While keeping their existing uniform design, the team ditched its black alternate jerseys in favor of a throwback inspired by the franchise’s inaugural 1966 uniforms. The throwbacks featured black jerseys, white pants, and the iconic red helmets with the original Falcons logo. Needless to say, these quickly became fan favorites.

Unfortunately, that look wouldn’t last long. In 2013, the NFL introduced its controversial “one-helmet rule,” which required teams to use the same helmet throughout the season as a precaution against concussions. This meant the Falcons could no longer wear their beloved red helmets, effectively shelving the throwbacks for several seasons. However, in 2016, the team brought them back with a slight modification: black helmets featuring the original Falcons logo instead of the traditional red ones. Although it wasn’t quite the same, it was certainly better than nothing.

The 2016 season also brought another interesting addition to the Falcons’ uniform history. The NFL expanded its “Color Rush” initiative, which featured specially designed, predominantly single-color uniforms for teams to wear during Thursday Night Football games. Atlanta unveiled an all-red combination that was originally expected to debut against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers that season. However, because both teams had red Color Rush uniforms, the Falcons were unable to wear theirs.

Instead, Atlanta finally debuted its all-red uniforms against the division-rival New Orleans Saints in 2017, a game the Falcons won 20–17. This would ultimately be the only time the team wore the combination. In 2018, the NFL discontinued the mandatory Color Rush program, although teams were still permitted to wear their Color Rush uniforms as alternates. Several teams continued doing so, but the Falcons weren’t among them.

Overall, the 2009–2019 era holds a special place in Falcons history, and for good reason. During this stretch, Atlanta experienced some of its greatest success as a franchise, including multiple playoff appearances, three NFC South titles, an NFC Championship, and a trip to Super Bowl LI. It was also the era of some of the greatest players to ever wear a Falcons uniform, including Matt Ryan and Julio Jones.

For many fans, these uniforms became synonymous with the most successful period in franchise history. Whether it was the iconic red jerseys worn during the team’s Super Bowl run or the classic black throwbacks, this era featured some of the most memorable looks and moments the franchise has ever produced.

2020-2025

In 2020, the Falcons underwent their first comprehensive uniform redesign since 2003, introducing a more modern look with several different combinations for their home and away uniforms. The redesign featured an enlarged helmet logo, a switch from black facemasks to silver, a new number font, and distinctive stripes running down the sides of the jerseys and pants. The team also returned to black as its primary home jersey color, while introducing black numbers on its white road jerseys in place of red. Personally, I think the black numbers were one of the best elements of the redesign, as they complemented the black helmets particularly well.

However, the new striping created some interesting complications. As you can see above, the Falcons originally unveiled red pants as part of their new uniform collection. The problem? Unlike the black and white pants, which featured red stripes to match the jerseys, the red pants featured black stripes. Since none of the jerseys had matching black stripes, the red pants didn’t exactly fit with the rest of the collection. Needless to say, the Falcons never actually wore them during a game.

The Falcons also introduced a rather controversial alternate uniform: the infamous red-to-black gradient jerseys. These featured a red upper half that gradually faded into black toward the waist, paired with black pants and the team’s black helmet. It was certainly a unique look, although whether it was a good look is another conversation entirely. The team wore these uniforms just three times: against the Detroit Lions (2020), New York Jets (2021), and Chicago Bears (2022). Ahead of the 2023 season, then-head coach Arthur Smith announced that the gradient jerseys would be shelved in favor of something much more familiar and beloved by fans: the classic red-helmet throwbacks.

Now, if you’re thinking, “Wait a second, didn’t you say earlier that the NFL had a one-helmet rule?” — you’d be correct. However, in 2021, the league announced that it would eliminate that restriction beginning with the 2022 season, allowing teams to introduce a second helmet for alternate and throwback uniforms. This opened the door for the Falcons to bring back their iconic red helmets, which hadn’t been worn since the 2012 season.

The red helmets officially returned in 2022, paired with the team’s classic black throwback jerseys and white pants. Beginning in 2023, the Falcons leaned further into that popular combination, choosing to wear the throwbacks more frequently rather than bringing back the gradient jerseys.

Overall, I’d argue that the 2020–2025 uniforms were among the least popular in franchise history. They were certainly a gamble, especially considering the previous uniform era had been the most successful in team history. Unfortunately, the Falcons never managed to build much success in their new look. Throughout these six seasons, Atlanta failed to make a single playoff appearance and never finished a season with more than eight wins.

2026-present

After six seasons with their controversial modern uniforms, the Falcons decided it was time for another change. On April 2, 2026, the Falcons officially unveiled a completely redesigned uniform set, returning to a more traditional look inspired by the franchise’s history. Perhaps the biggest change was the return of red as the team’s primary home jersey color, something that hadn’t been the case since the 2019 season.

Unlike the previous uniforms, which featured oversized “ATL” lettering, unusual number fonts, and bold side striping, the new design takes a much simpler approach. The home jerseys are once again red with white numbers, while the away jerseys returned to having red numbers. The Falcons also introduced a more traditional number font, with subtle angles inspired by the team’s logo. The oversized “ATL” lettering is gone, replaced by smaller “FALCONS” lettering on the home jerseys and “ATLANTA” on the away jerseys. The team’s logo also returns to a more prominent position on the sleeves.

Another interesting addition is the increased use of silver, a color that has been part of the Falcons’ identity for decades. The new pants feature stripes combining silver, white, black, and red, inspired by the franchise’s original 1966 uniforms. Both white and black pants are available, giving the Falcons several combinations to choose from throughout the season.

The helmets also received a few subtle updates. Atlanta retained its black helmets and modern Falcons logo, but introduced a low-gloss finish and a more traditional silver facemask. It’s not a drastic change, but the adjustments help tie the entire uniform together. Of course, one question many fans had leading up to the unveiling was whether the Falcons would keep the red-helmet throwbacks in the rotation. Thankfully, the team confirmed that the classic 1966-inspired throwbacks would remain.

Overall, I think the 2026 redesign is a significant improvement over the previous uniforms. The Falcons managed to combine elements of their past with a cleaner, more modern look without trying to reinvent the wheel. The return of red jerseys is especially welcome, and the simpler design feels like something that could stand the test of time.

Whether these uniforms become as iconic as some of the franchise’s previous looks remains to be seen, but one thing is certain: the Falcons have returned to a more traditional identity, and hopefully, this new era brings some much-needed success on the field as well.

Personally, I’m hoping the Falcons eventually add a black alternate jersey to the mix. And if I’m not getting too greedy, I’d love to see the return of silver pants to complement the silver facemasks. That would really complete the look, in my opinion.
